mathcounts-potw-2025-12-15-01.title: Person by person
mathcounts-potw-2025-12-15-01.body:
Cousin 1; grandmother $3 + 1 = 4$; grandfather $2 \times 1.5 = 3$; mother $2 + 3 = 5$; father $1 + 3 = 4$. Total $1 + 4 + 3 + 5 + 4 = 17$.

**Answer: 17**

mathcounts-potw-2025-12-15-02.title: Round up each color
mathcounts-potw-2025-12-15-02.body:
- Color 1: $200 \div 150 \approx 1.33$ → 2 balls.
- Color 2: $800 \div 150 \approx 5.33$ → 6 balls.
- Color 3: $1300 - 1000 = 300$ yards, $300 \div 150 = 2$ balls.

Total $2 + 6 + 2 = 10$.

**Answer: 10**

mathcounts-potw-2025-12-15-02.title: Why not 9?
mathcounts-potw-2025-12-15-02.body:
$1300 \div 150 \approx 8.67$ would suggest 9 balls, but each color must be bought separately in whole balls. Colors 1 and 2 each leave part of a ball unused, so 10 balls are needed.

**Answer: 10**

mathcounts-potw-2025-12-15-03.title: Try the largest scarf counts
mathcounts-potw-2025-12-15-03.body:
With $h \ge 1$ hats, $p \ge 1$ pairs of socks and $s$ scarves: $h + 1.5p + 3s = 18$.

- $s = 5$: $h + 1.5p = 3$. $p = 1$ gives $h = 1.5$ (not whole); $p = 2$ gives $h = 0$ (not allowed). ✗
- $s = 4$: $h + 1.5p = 6$. $p = 2$, $h = 3$ works ✓.

So the largest number is **4** scarves (with 3 hats and 2 pairs of socks).

**Answer: 4**

mathcounts-potw-2025-12-15-03.title: Parity argument
mathcounts-potw-2025-12-15-03.body:
Socks must come in an even number of pairs (otherwise the half ball can't be used up), so socks use a multiple of 3 balls; with at least 2 pairs that is at least 3 balls. Scarves also use multiples of 3. So hats use $18 - (\text{multiple of }3)$, a multiple of 3, which is at least 3. That leaves at most $18 - 3 - 3 = 12$ balls for scarves: $12 \div 3 = 4$.

**Answer: 4**
